title: Pressure support level versus VT and RR in a spontaneous patient
subtitle: Effect of inspiratory pressure support on tidal volume, work of breathing, and ventilation in spontaneous breathing
ruleBasedNote: Effort unloading by pressure support is a rule-based relationship in Engine v1.

patient.summary: A 50-year-old spontaneously breathing patient recovering from acute lung injury undergoing a pressure support weaning trial.

prediction.question: When pressure support above PEEP is increased from 5 to 16 cmH2O, how do exhaled tidal volume (VTE), peak airway pressure (Ppeak), and arterial PaCO2 respond?

whatToLookAtHint: Observe the exhaled tidal volume (VTE), peak airway pressure on the ventilator, and arterial carbon dioxide tension.

reflection.question: How does increasing pressure support level alter the patient's respiratory pattern and work of breathing?

options.text: Greater inspiratory pressure assistance increases the transpulmonary pressure gradient, expanding delivered tidal volume and unburdening patient inspiratory muscles, which increases alveolar ventilation and lowers PaCO2.
Pressure support enforces a fixed delivered volume regardless of patient effort, converting the breath to mandatory volume control.
Increasing pressure support level reduces neural inspiratory drive below the apnoea threshold, producing severe hypoventilation.
Pressure support alters expiratory triggering resistance only, without modifying peak pressure or delivered tidal volume.

reflection.explanation: In pressure support ventilation (PSV), the ventilator assists each patient-triggered breath up to the set target pressure (PEEP + PS). Increasing PS from 5 to 16 cmH2O raises peak airway pressure from 10 to 21 cmH2O. This larger pressure gradient inflates the lung with a significantly greater tidal volume (from ~455 mL to ~732 mL). As mechanical support unloads the respiratory muscles, total alveolar ventilation rises and arterial PaCO2 falls from ~38 to ~31 mmHg, moderately dampening chemoreflex respiratory drive.

evidence.claim: Pressure support ventilation reduces the patient's work of breathing in proportion to the level of pressure assistance by increasing tidal volume and unloading respiratory muscles.
evidence.source: Brochard L. Pressure support ventilation. In: Tobin MJ, ed. Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation. 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill; 2013:227-248.

evidence.claim: Titration of inspiratory pressure support modifies tidal volume, respiratory rate, and PaCO2 according to respiratory system compliance and patient effort.
evidence.source: MacIntyre NR. Respiratory mechanics in the patient-ventilator system. Respir Care 2005; 50(2):238-245.
